summary.text: 很 is built from 彳 and 艮: 彳 is the semantic element, and 艮 supplies an approximate sound cue. Its common meaning is “very; quite”; older glosses include “not obeying,” “difficult to walk,” and “perverse,” but how these uses relate is uncertain.

formation.text: This is a phonosemantic compound, combining semantic 彳 with phonetic 艮. The Shuowen glosses include “not obeying,” “difficult to walk,” and “perverse”; the evidence does not establish how those senses are related or exactly how 彳 contributes.

components.text: 彳 is the semantic component in 很. Its precise contribution to the early glosses is not clear.
艮 is the phonetic component. Its Old Chinese reconstruction resembles 很’s, though the forms differ; this sound role does not identify 艮’s oldest referent or name.

sound_limitation.text: The cited sound comparison supports an approximate relationship but does not establish 艮’s original referent or name.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang Shangfang’s Old Chinese reconstruction, 艮 *kɯːns and 很 *ɡɯːnʔ are similar but differ in initial, final, and tone. Their modern Mandarin readings, gèn and hěn, also differ.

history.text: The available graphic record identifies a Shuowen small-seal form for 很 but does not provide an earlier sequence. The curated image shows 艮 in a modern seal-script-style rendering; it is the proposed sound component, not an early form of 很.

uncertainties.text: The early glosses “not obeying,” “difficult to walk,” and “perverse” are not securely ordered. One dictionary proposes “difficult to walk” as the original sense, but the connection is uncertain.

The development of the degree use is disputed: proposals include grammaticalization from adjectival 很/狠 constructions and Yuan-period contact involving a degree word written 哏. The first use’s date and textual witness remain unresolved.

senses.text: Reference works record adjectival uses meaning fierce or perverse. One scholarly account places this adjective after earlier noncompliance usage, though the chronology is uncertain.

senses.text: 很 commonly means “very” or “quite.” Its development has been explained as grammaticalization from adjectival constructions or as connected with Yuan-period contact and a degree word written 哏; the route is unsettled.

developments.text: A scholarly account proposes that the sense of noncompliance developed into a fierce or cruel adjective; this sequence is not a verified chronology.

The degree use may have developed through adjectival constructions, or may be connected with a contact-related degree use written 哏. The evidence does not settle whether this was semantic change, grammaticalization, or adoption of a related spoken form with changing spellings.

limitations.text: The early glosses are not securely ordered, and a continuous semantic chain from difficulty or defiance to the modern degree use is not established.
The first degree use’s precise date, reading, and textual witness remain unresolved; the reported Yuan example comes from article notes rather than an independently inspected primary witness.

overview.text: 很 means “very” or “quite” today. It combines semantic 彳 with 艮 as an approximate sound cue: their reconstructed Old Chinese forms are similar but not identical. Older glosses concern disobedience or difficulty; their relation to the modern degree use is uncertain.

components.text: 彳 is the semantic part of 很, though its exact contribution to the early glosses is unclear.
艮 is a sound cue: its reconstructed Old Chinese form resembles 很’s, though the two forms differ.

takeaway.text: The modern “very; quite” meaning is not a proven direct development from “defiant” or “difficult to walk.”

relationships.text: 彳 is analyzed as the semantic component in 很, though its specific contribution to the early glosses remains unclear.
艮 is analyzed as the phonetic component; the cited Old Chinese reconstructions show an approximate, nonidentical sound relationship.
